evidence_items.publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER Digest)

receipt.public_excerpt: More than 90 percent of executives report no effect of AI use on employment over the past three years, and 89 percent report no impact on labor productivity. Among the minority that do report effects, the results tilt slightly positive for productivity, with an estimated average boost of 0.29 percent.

evidence_items.explanation: A survey of nearly 6,000 executives (Nov 2025–Jan 2026) found that most firms saw no productivity effect from AI. That points to a small real-world impact so far.

evidence_items.locator: Section 'Generative AI’s Projected Impact on TFP', paragraph 1

receipt.public_excerpt: we estimate that AI’s impact on TFP growth remains small today - 0.01 percentage points (pp) in 2025 - as most businesses have yet to deploy and gain experience with AI tools.

evidence_items.explanation: Penn Wharton estimates AI added almost nothing to economy-wide productivity growth in 2025.

receipt.public_excerpt: they could drive a 7% (or almost $7 trillion) increase in global GDP and lift productivity growth by 1.5 percentage points over a 10-year period.

evidence_items.explanation: An example of the large, widely cited expectations. It covers a 10-year span, so it is not strictly falsified yet.

receipt.public_excerpt: executives report AI adoption has raised annual labor productivity growth by 0.2% over the last 3 years, a modest impact, but expect a substantially larger 0.6% per annum boost over the next 3 years.

evidence_items.explanation: A later survey wave (Summer 2026) again finds a modest effect so far. It is dated after the post, so it is context only.

unresolved_gaps: US nonfarm productivity growth was strong in parts of 2025. Some commentators credited AI, but the attribution is disputed and I did not read a primary source on it.
It is hard to pin down exactly what 'many people' expected for the period up to mid-2026.
